title: Deep neck space infection and Ludwig angina
subtitle: Including peritonsillar abscess: the airway first, then the pus

sources.title: Diagnosis and management of Ludwig's angina: an evidence-based review (Bridwell et al.)

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Sore throat (acute): antimicrobial prescribing (NG84)
Difficult Airway Society guidelines for awake tracheal intubation (ATI) in adults

red_flags.text: Stridor, drooling, inability to swallow saliva, or a patient who insists on sitting up: the airway is threatened now.
Ludwig angina: firm bilateral submandibular swelling with a raised, tender floor of mouth and the tongue pushed up and back.
Trismus with a muffled 'hot potato' voice and deviation of the uvula: peritonsillar abscess, or a parapharyngeal abscess if the neck is also swollen.
Neck stiffness or torticollis with fever in a child: retropharyngeal abscess.
Chest pain, mediastinal widening or sepsis with a neck infection: descending necrotising mediastinitis.
Unilateral neck swelling and tenderness along the sternocleidomastoid after a sore throat, with septic emboli to the lungs: Lemierre syndrome.

do_now.text: Assess the airway first and call the senior anaesthetist and senior ENT surgeon at once for any airway sign. Keep the patient upright and with them.
No sedation and no lying flat for a scan in a patient with any airway sign until the airway plan is agreed.
Intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics covering streptococci and anaerobes per local protocol, started without waiting for imaging.
Refer to hospital any sore throat with severe systemic illness or a suspected suppurative complication such as quinsy, parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal abscess.

assess.text: Dental examination: most Ludwig angina comes from the lower molar teeth, whose roots lie below the mylohyoid line.
Trismus and the degree of mouth opening, which tells the anaesthetist whether a laryngoscope will fit.
Flexible nasendoscopy, with the airway team present, to see the supraglottis and the pharyngeal wall.
Sepsis screen and severity scores. Diabetes and immunosuppression are common and worsen the course.
Peritonsillar abscess versus cellulitis: a fluctuant bulge above and lateral to the tonsil with uvular deviation suggests pus.

investigate.text: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, and of the chest if mediastinal spread is possible, once the airway is safe or the patient is accompanied by someone who can secure it.
Blood cultures, full blood count, renal function, glucose and inflammatory markers.
Orthopantomogram or the dental windows on the CT to identify the source tooth.
A peritonsillar abscess does not need a CT routinely. Image when the abscess may extend beyond the peritonsillar space or the diagnosis is unclear.

resuscitate.text: Fluid resuscitation and sepsis care in parallel with airway planning.
Intravenous corticosteroid is used in many units to reduce airway oedema, though the evidence base is limited. Follow local protocol.

definitive.text: Secure the airway in theatre with awake fibreoptic intubation or awake tracheostomy under local anaesthesia when the airway is threatened, with the neck marked and a surgeon scrubbed.

Surgical drainage of the involved spaces with removal of the source tooth for Ludwig angina with a collection or a deteriorating patient. Early cellulitis without pus may settle with antibiotics under close observation.
Peritonsillar abscess: needle aspiration or incision and drainage under local anaesthesia, with antibiotics and analgesia so the patient can swallow.
Parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal abscesses with a collection on CT usually need surgical drainage, transorally or through the neck, under general anaesthesia with a secured airway.
Mediastinal extension needs cardiothoracic surgery for drainage. Neck drainage alone is not enough.

escalate.text: Senior ENT, senior anaesthetist and critical care for any deep neck infection with airway signs.
Maxillofacial or dental surgery for an odontogenic source. Cardiothoracic surgery for mediastinitis.
Transfer a patient with a threatened airway only after it is secured, or with airway-competent staff and equipment in the vehicle.

notes: Ludwig angina is a cellulitis of the floor of the mouth that kills through the airway. The infection is treated with antibiotics and surgery; the patient survives because of the airway plan.
Trismus in a peritonsillar abscess is from muscle spasm and often improves after drainage, but trismus with neck swelling is a parapharyngeal abscess until imaged.
The scanner is a dangerous place for a patient with a threatened airway. Secure it, or bring the team.
